A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching core theory and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across appendix moves and figure renumbering.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendix B report original corpus statistics, transformer training results, scaling curves, and within-horizon learning analyses on TinyStories and WikiText.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds non-transformer comparisons, exponent-sensitivity analyses, and fitted learning-curve confidence intervals.

M1.justification: The prediction-horizon construction, scaling-exponent formula αD = γ/(2β), and underlying training approach remain unchanged. Added architectures serve as comparators; mathematical corrections and uncertainty analyses do not introduce a new proposed learning procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate next-token language modeling on TinyStories and WikiText-103. Additional architecture comparisons and exponent sweeps remain within this dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 2 adds Mamba and infini-gram, labeled N-gram in the plot, to the retained GPT-2 APE, GPT-2 RoPE, and LLaMA comparison. This substantially broadens the entropy-independence test beyond transformer architectures to two different model families.

E3.justification: Section 4.2.3 and Appendix C.3 introduce empirical-exponent estimation from the lower envelope across context lengths, fitting its first m points for varying m. The retained experiments' tokenization, evaluation splits, model configurations, and optimization grids are unchanged; newly specified fitting windows do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's within-horizon decay analysis and architecture/context comparisons, v3 adds systematic β and γ sensitivity tests in Figures 8–12 and learning-curve fitting-window checks in Appendix C.3. These directly test the stability of the central validation and identify a LLaMA-specific collapse discrepancy.

E5.justification: v1 reports language-exponent point estimates without the uncertainty analysis introduced in v3. Section 4.2.3 and Appendix C add bootstrap errors for β and γ, propagated uncertainty for αD, and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for empirical scaling exponents. These are estimation procedures, not evidence of additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: TinyStories γ changes from 0.34 to 0.325. New results include Mamba/infini-gram entropy curves, LLaMA autoregressive scaling in Figure 17, sensitivity findings, and the Appendix C.3 interval table; displayed T=64 results are omitted. The table's TinyStories intervals overlap the predicted interval even at m=11–12, although Section 4.2.3 highlights overlap only through ten points.

T1.justification: New Appendix B derives the P^(-1/2) covariance-noise scale under independent-pair and fixed-vocabulary assumptions, using matrix concentration and singular-value bounds; v1 states this scale without that derivation. Appendix A also corrects the collapse derivation to retain H∞ and changes the telescoping sums' lower limit from 2 to 1.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claim: language correlation and conditional-entropy statistics predict data-limited scaling exponents without free fitting parameters, supported by TinyStories and WikiText experiments. Additional evidence does not redefine this headline contribution.

C2.justification: v3 introduces an important qualification to the collapse interpretation: LLaMA's collapse appears sharper at β around 0.6–0.7 than at the independently measured 0.88 ± 0.06, despite compatible autoregressive scaling. It leaves this discrepancy unresolved and additionally distinguishes fitting-window uncertainty from statistical error and explains optimization/context constraints on exponent estimation.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v3 supplies a specific repository described as containing training code, data, and figure scripts. Appendices C and E additionally specify essential exponent-fitting windows and sampling grids, plus Mamba's architecture and optimization settings. These substantially improve documented reproducibility; repository contents were not independently inspected.

R1.justification: v3 connects conditional-entropy decay to Hilberg's hypothesis and prior entropy measurements, expands discussion of Zipf/quanta-based theories, and adds references for the new comparators and spectral detectability argument. These extend the existing positioning while preserving the claimed contribution relative to prior scaling-law theories.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose are retained. Changes include localized explanations, a new error-estimates subsection, inserted sampling-noise and uncertainty appendices, conference front matter, and an Impact Statement; the original narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v3 adds uncertainty/sensitivity Figures 7–12 and an exponent-comparison table, merges v1 Figures 8–9 into Figure 14, and adds an autoregressive panel to the LLaMA figure. Legends, color scales, and supporting displays also change. T=64 panels disappear, although Figure 15's caption still lists that setting.

improvement.justification: v1's central quantitative agreement relies heavily on point estimates and visual comparisons. v3 substantially improves its assessability through uncertainty estimates, fitting-window and collapse-sensitivity tests, and an explicit conditional derivation of the sampling-noise scale. Broader entropy comparisons and concrete reproducibility information strengthen that improvement. The unresolved LLaMA discrepancy and caption/table-summary inconsistencies limit the validation, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support and transparency.
